translations.text: But it is fitting that we should briefly bring in here the memory of the holy and spotless hierarch and martyr,
to whom was rightly granted the honour of the hope that had been prepared, the throne of glory,
most exalted among the righteous for his great holiness, and above all others martyred for the truth,
confirming it with his own blood. He offered himself as a sacrifice to Him who redeemed us with His own blood.
He set upon himself the crown of victory, seizing it himself and flying up on high, he who the fruits [?].
brought forth from his own self, with the help of the Most High, the sixtyfold of holiness and the hundredfold of martyrdom,
and by joining these with his own self he was found to be the one who completed the sevenfold [?]: that hierarch of grace,
mediator between God and men, the blessed Abibos, bishop of the city of Nekresi, who stood forth in both ranks of the assembly of the saints.
He took his throne among the spotless successors to the throne of the priesthood, and he also hastened to the contest with the valiant martyrs and swiftly carried off the prize of the race,
and he was found among those honoured with a crown, among the zealots, the righteous ones of the law.
This martyr is mine and no one else's, from this see of mine: a beautiful fruit that brings me joy, a white rose that makes the air fragrant
and spreads its fragrance over me. He lit his lamp upon a high mountain, so that the whole world might see that unquenchable light, which shines in two ways.
He offered to God the very flesh of the Word without beginning, and at last he offered himself upon that same blessed altar
as a whole burnt offering to Him. He was offered by the hand of that lawless marzpan, who indeed offered him up.
Now, beloved, I want you to know the cause of this matter. The king of the Persians had seized Kartli, and they were the rulers of this land of ours,
and they were always practising that foul idolatry, the worship and service of fire,
that Babylonian custom: some worshipped gold, others something else, and at times fire, from time to time, as they were burned [?] by their own evil teacher, the devil.
For this reason they set up many places in the land for the worship of their fire, and they led many people of weak understanding astray into an unfounded faith.
But the blessed Abibos, bishop of the city of Nekresi, in the valley of Kakheti,
was stirred with divine zeal and could not bear to have that alien worship near him. He poured a little water [?] on it and put it out.
When the lawless Persians learned of this, they beat the blessed man severely, almost to death, and shut him up in prison in great hardship and with many tortures.
After this they quickly wrote about the matter to the marzpan in the upper country. He ordered that he be bound at once and brought before him.
The tormentors who had been sent came and took him away as they had been ordered, and they brought him with many kinds of affliction.
Now the blessed bishop Abibos was a friend of that brilliant luminary, Symeon the Stylite of Antioch. It was not that they had ever seen each other in person,
but through that spiritual love by which someone far away is seen as if near. They also kept in contact with each other by letter and by messenger.
At that very time, while holy Abibos was being led away, the messenger of holy Simeon the Stylite met him at a village
called Ialdo. He brought him a letter as a blessing (eulogia), and the staff of holy Simeon the Stylite of Antioch, the wonder-worker.
When the bishop received the letter, he read it. He took the blessing and the staff, rejoiced with great joy, and was greatly strengthened.
He took them with him and came on cheerfully, even though it was possible for him not to come.
Even those who were leading him agreed and said to him: "If you do not wish to go, we will release you and send you back."
But he would not accept this, because he was in haste and longed for martyrdom.
When they came near this royal city of ours, Mtskheta, he called out to his mother Rachel, which is the one catholic and apostolic church.
And while he was still speaking, he said: "Mother, behold, your son Joseph is being led to Egypt in bonds, like a captive." And it was as if someone said to him:
"Not so; rather, you are being made ready to reign, from those beautiful fruits, from his own treasures." [He answered:] "That way of yours pleases me, and may I walk on it." [?]
Then he begged the torturers to let him go to the cave of the blessed Shio, for he had known him before and longed to see him.
They let him go, and he went down into the desert and saw that blessed elder.
They prayed and greeted one another. As they talked, the holy bishop said to the elder:
"Pray, father, for these lawless Persians have grown furious against us in their arrogance, since they have seized this land of ours.
You know that Babylon always makes burnt offerings to idols, and its people look for ways to make all men worship idols.
Once, the three youths, with the Son of God standing beside them, melted that idol and destroyed it by his own power, and brought the tyrant with all his might down under shame.
And now his lawless followers, after his example, mean to spread the net again, catch men in it, and make them worship fire."
The elder answered and said: "I know, lord father, that you completely quenched their fire, in which those lawless men trusted.
But may the Lord grant you to quench easily that invisible fire as well, which the devil has kindled against you to test you.
Your holiness is not ignorant that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations.
But do not tremble at their tyranny, for the apostle says: 'Affliction to those who afflict you, and relief to you who are afflicted.'
Know that the affliction they bring will become unfading glory for you, and that affliction of yours will become their fall and scattering."
After much talk, blessed Abibos was strengthened by the elder. They prayed, and he set out joyfully for his contest.
They brought him to the marzpan at the upper village, the village called Rekhi.
A multitude of bishops, priests and nobles gathered there, and a great spectacle took place before the marzpan.
Then they brought forward holy Abibos the bishop, and the marzpan said to him: "Why did you reject the authority of the King of Kings and kill our god?"
Abibos answered and said to him: "I know no one as king except our Lord Jesus Christ. As for the fire, I put it out so that I might dispel the devil's deception.
"But I beg you to turn away from that worthless worship and to know God alone, by whom all things were created,
"and to serve him alone, for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone."
The marzpan said to him: "I am asking why you killed your god, and yet you want to lead us over to your own god?"
But the blessed Abibos said to him: "Let it be known to you that I have not killed a god; I put out a fire.
"That is not a god. It is one of the other elements, a small part of a single substance, one of those out of which God set up this world.
"The moist, the cold, the dry and fire were created in balance, and they hold one another in check within that sphere.
"So they stand through the balance of their parts, and if one had grown greater than another, the other would have perished.
"And that fire of yours is a part of that same element of fire, together with the dry and the cold, and it rises up by consuming wood over a long time.
"I poured a little water on it, and the water overpowered it and killed it, because the water proved greater than it.
"Now I am amazed at this madness of yours: how are you not ashamed to call it god, a thing that has so much
"breath [?]? For this fire of yours is your own slave, and it cannot see any of those who insult the idols, if it is a god!
"You say that once, in your own land, you prepared the worship of that idol, the one you made of gold.
"That which you prepared back then as an instrument of torture is now called a god!?"
Then the king's marzpan grew very angry. After much beating and terrible tortures, they crushed the head of the blessed Abibos with stones, killed him, and dragged him outside the city.
Guards were posted over him so that beasts and birds would eat his flesh, for the marzpan was afraid that the Christians might come, take him away, and bury him with honour.
But none of the beasts or birds touched the body of that thrice-blessed man at all.
After the guards had kept watch for a long time, they left and went away. Then the fathers who lived around the towns of Rekhi came out,
one of whose disciples had built that monastery, and they took up the relics of holy Abibos and buried them in that place with great honour.
And so holy Abibos was offered up as a holy sacrifice, and one could rightly say:
"He is a namesake of Zechariah, the father of John, not in name but in likeness: the lot of the priesthood fell to Zechariah, and his blood too was shed in holiness."
In telling you this about the blessed bishop Abibos, I am not reporting to you all his deeds, labours and struggles,
such as how he smashed the idols, brought the godless to believe in Christ, and baptized them in the name of the Holy Trinity,
or how he foretold to that woman that the Greeks would come soon after his own death and conquer this land of ours, which came to pass quickly.
In that same woman's lifetime the Greeks came, drove out those lawless Persians, and took this land of ours.
From that time on the eristavs (heads of the people) became rulers of Kartli, along with many others, as is written in the book of his martyrdom.
But I want to tell you, brothers, that these earthly angels, lights of the world, vessels full of fragrant ointment,
who by their own courage adorned this world of ours at one and the same time, were like a golden chain, linked one to another:
the holy bishop Abibos of Nekresi, the blessed John of Zedazeni, Ise, bishop of Tsilkani, remembered with honour, and, with grace
filled, the elder Shio, along with the other disciples of that same blessed John of Zedazeni, who adorned the Church with their beautiful way of life.
One of them built Alaverdi, from which great wonders and many healings come forth to this very day, renowned throughout the whole surrounding land.
Another founded the cave of Iulta, others planted monasteries in Kukheti, and one founded the desert of Gareja and performed many wonders.
And one built a monastery in Zena-Sopeli and established this sign: that no female creature should enter it.
He made the birds of the sky and the creeping things obey his word, so that they would not dare to nest in it, as our own eyes see today.
And since all the places of those saints are adorned and flourish today, if anyone did not believe in their unseen glory,
how would he understand from their places the boldness they have before the Lord!? But I cannot mention all those others.
Instead, by this brief account let us come to know that great thing, let us taste from the holy springs, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
Now the blessed Shio found in the cave that heavenly pearl. He took it into himself, made it dwell there, and hastened to go before Him
whom he had acquired. He brought him to the place for which he longed, and he went to his rest in great glory. And a multitude of monks gathered there.
According to custom, they buried his body in that place and appointed the feast of that blessed man in the fifth [week] of Easter,
on the Lord's day (Sunday). After this the holy Evagrius, who struggled well, went down into that cave,
so that he would not leave his teacher's place empty and would become heir to his virtues, which he carried out in deed.
